title: The Chief Series of A₄ Made Explicit: A₄ ▷ V₄ ▷ 1 (factors ℤ/3ℤ and (ℤ/2ℤ)²)
description: Answers the parent's open question by exhibiting the classical chief series of A₄ explicitly in Lean, with both chief factors identified with their standard models: the top factor A₄/V₄ ≅ ℤ/3ℤ (cyclic of prime order 3) and the bottom factor V₄ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)² (the Klein four-group). Note this is a chief (solvable) series, not a composition series: the bottom factor V₄ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)² is abelian but not simple, so it refines further (V₄ ▷ C₂ ▷ 1) to reach the genuine composition series A₄ ▷ V₄ ▷ C₂ ▷ 1 with simple factors ℤ/3ℤ, ℤ/2ℤ, ℤ/2ℤ. Where the parent proves A₄ solvable indirectly (as a subgroup of solvable S₄, or by collapsing its second derived subgroup), this entry displays the abelian layers directly. Assembled axiom-free from Mathlib's alternatingGroup.kleinFour infrastructure: V₄ ◁ A₄ is normal, |A₄|=12 and |V₄|=4 give |A₄/V₄|=3 by Lagrange, mulEquivOfPrimeCardEq turns prime order 3 into the cyclic isomorphism, and IsKleinFour.nonempty_mulEquiv identifies V₄ with (ℤ/2ℤ)². Since V₄ is exactly the commutator subgroup, the displayed chain is precisely the derived series of A₄.

overview.historicalContext: Galois (1846) linked solvability by radicals to solvability of the Galois group; Jordan (1870) first studied composition series of alternating and symmetric groups systematically. A₄ is the largest alternating group that is solvable, and its chief series A₄ ▷ V₄ ▷ 1 — with the Klein four-group V₄ as the unique nontrivial proper normal subgroup — is the textbook example of a non-trivial solvable series. (It is a chief, not a composition, series: the bottom factor V₄ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)² is abelian but not simple, so the genuine composition series is the refinement A₄ ▷ V₄ ▷ C₂ ▷ 1.) The parent gallery entry proves A₄ solvable but obtains solvability indirectly (via S₄ or a derived-series collapse); this entry instead exhibits the classical series with its abelian factors named, which is what 'A₄ is solvable' means structurally.
overview.problemStatement: Exhibit the chief (solvable) series A₄ ▷ V₄ ▷ {e} explicitly in Lean, with the quotient isomorphisms A₄/V₄ ≅ ℤ/3ℤ and V₄ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)² identified.
overview.text: V₄ = alternatingGroup.kleinFour (Fin 4) is the subgroup generated by the (2,2)-cycle-type permutations; it is normal in A₄ (normal_kleinFour) and equals the commutator subgroup (kleinFour_eq_commutator), so A₄ ▷ V₄ ▷ 1 is the derived series. Lagrange gives the factor orders: |A₄| = 4!/2 = 12 and |V₄| = 4, so |A₄/V₄| = 3. The top factor A₄/V₄ has prime order 3, hence is cyclic (isCyclic_of_prime_card) and isomorphic to Multiplicative (ZMod 3) via mulEquivOfPrimeCardEq. The bottom factor V₄ is a Klein four-group (kleinFour_isKleinFour: order 4, exponent 2), and any two Klein four-groups are isomorphic (IsKleinFour.nonempty_mulEquiv), so V₄ ≅ Multiplicative (ZMod 2 × ZMod 2). Both factors are abelian, so this is a solvable (chief) series and A₄ is solvable — re-derived constructively from the displayed layers. It is not yet a composition series: the bottom factor V₄ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)² has order 4 and is not simple, so refining V₄ ▷ ⟨t⟩ ▷ 1 yields the true composition series A₄ ▷ V₄ ▷ C₂ ▷ 1 with the three simple factors ℤ/3ℤ, ℤ/2ℤ, ℤ/2ℤ.
overview.proofStrategy: Pure assembly from Mathlib's dedicated alternating-group / Klein-four API. Establish the base hypothesis Nat.card (Fin 4) = 4, feed it to the kleinFour lemmas for normality and cardinalities, get |A₄/V₄| = 3 from Lagrange, then convert prime order to a cyclic isomorphism and Klein-four-ness to the (ℤ/2ℤ)² isomorphism.
keyInsights: The chief factors are identified with concrete models, not just shown abelian: A₄/V₄ ≅ ℤ/3ℤ and V₄ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)². This is the difference between 'A₄ is solvable' and 'here is A₄'s solvable series with its layers named'. (These are chief factors, not composition factors: V₄ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)² is not simple, so a composition series would refine it into two ℤ/2ℤ layers.)
V₄ equals the commutator subgroup [A₄, A₄], so the exhibited series IS the derived series — the two standard descriptions of A₄'s solvability coincide on the nose.
The top factor is handled by a cardinality argument alone: prime order 3 forces cyclic, and mulEquivOfPrimeCardEq produces the ℤ/3ℤ isomorphism without exhibiting a generator by hand.
The bottom factor is handled by the IsKleinFour mixin: order 4 + exponent 2 characterizes the Klein four-group up to isomorphism, so V₄ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)² needs no explicit element matching.
Both isomorphisms are stated as Multiplicative (ZMod n) because the ambient groups are written multiplicatively; Multiplicative (ZMod n) is the group ℤ/nℤ presented multiplicatively.
prerequisites: The alternating group A₄ and its Klein four subgroup
Cyclic groups of prime order (isCyclic_of_prime_card, mulEquivOfPrimeCardEq)
The Klein four-group as order-4 exponent-2 (IsKleinFour)

conclusion.summary: The classical chief (solvable) series of A₄ is exhibited explicitly: A₄ ▷ V₄ ▷ 1 with V₄ ◁ A₄ normal (= the commutator subgroup), the top factor A₄/V₄ ≅ ℤ/3ℤ, and the bottom factor V₄ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)². Both factors abelian, so A₄ is solvable, constructively. This is a chief series, not a composition series — V₄ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)² is not simple, so the true composition series is the refinement A₄ ▷ V₄ ▷ C₂ ▷ 1. 11 theorems, 135 lines, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: This turns the parent's indirect solvability proof into the textbook chief series with named abelian layers, and shows the derived series and the chief series of A₄ coincide (V₄ = [A₄, A₄]). (The genuine composition series A₄ ▷ V₄ ▷ C₂ ▷ 1 is one refinement step longer, since V₄ is not simple.) It provides a reusable pattern for identifying small quotient/subgroup factors with standard models (prime-order ⟹ cyclic via mulEquivOfPrimeCardEq; order-4 exponent-2 ⟹ Klein four via IsKleinFour).
openQuestions: Assemble the data into Mathlib's CompositionSeries structure and prove the factors are the simple groups ℤ/3ℤ, ℤ/2ℤ, ℤ/2ℤ (refining V₄ ▷ ⟨t⟩ ▷ 1).
Contrast with A₅, whose only composition series is A₅ ▷ 1 with the simple non-abelian factor A₅ — the structural reason A₅ (and hence Sₙ, n ≥ 5) is not solvable.
Relate the ℤ/3ℤ top factor to the resolvent cubic of the general quartic, making the S₄ ▷ A₄ ▷ V₄ ▷ ... series the group-theoretic shadow of the classical quartic solution.
